catalog_quote: Fore has only one phonemic suprasegmental feature: pitch-accent, to which I shall refer simply as 'accent'. As in a stress system, the unit of accent placement is the syllable, even though the main diagnostic feature of Fore accent is pitch. An accented syllable incurs higher pitch, which may be either level or falling. ... Each morpheme has its own underlying accent patterning. The surface realisation of accent in words results from the combination of these underlying patterns. [p.20] There are two components to a morpheme's underlying accent. Firstly, a morpheme may be accented on one of its syllable nuclei, or it may be completely unaccented. Two accents on a single morpheme occur, but never on adjacent syllables. Secondly, a morpheme may induce an accent on a following syllable ... This induced accent may be the sole distinguishing factor between otherwise homophonous forms ... [p.2…
sweep_summary: Fore (fore1270, catalog: tonal/pitch accent, Scott 1978). Four works with stress in the title = three works: (1)+(2) Pike & Scott 1963 ZPSK/STUF 16:179-189, the dedicated pitch accent analysis, duplicated in Glottolog; paywalled at De Gruyter (DOI 10.1524/stuf.1963.16.14.179), online with a university library loginvia the Harvard library catalogue; Scott 1978 fn.28/p.22 summarise it (stress-type system cued by pitch not intensity) — medium priority, would deepen evidence, not change coding. (3) Scott 1990 'A reanalysis of Fore accent', La Trobe WP in Linguistics 3:139-150, not in our bibliography and not obtainable today (SIL PNG archive id 48692 down; no Crossref/OA record found) — HIGH priority: same analyst's later reanalysis is the one item that could refine or change the classification. (4) Pilch 1970 Kivung 3(2):133-142, held by the project and read (scanned): secondary argument that the Fore 'accent' is distinctive word-stress realised by pitch; no placement data; Scott 1978 p.22 rebuts his 'three patterns' claim — refines label only. Best statement read remains the deciding source itself (Scott 1978 §2.31.1 pp.19-20, verbatim in held text); catalog's classification confirmed, nothing supersedes it. archive.

new_statements.citation: Scott, Graham. 1978. The Fore language of Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-47. Canberra: Australian National University. (CC BY-SA 4.0 online edition, sealang.net/CRCL) — §2.31.1 'Description' (of Accent), pp. 19-20; §2.32 p. 23
new_statements.reading: This is the catalog's own deciding source, re-read verbatim in the copy we hold: Fore has lexically specified pitch accent (per-morpheme underlying accent, including unaccented and post-accenting morphemes), with surface restraints (max two adjacent accents; no word-initial adjacent accents except disyllables in isolation), no weight or edge rule, and 'No contrastive intonation patterns occur' (p. 23). Nothing read in this search of works with stress in the title supersedes it: the only newly read item, Pilch 1970, is a secondary terminological argument (call it distinctive word-stress realised by pitch) that Scott 1978 p. 22 already addresses; the dedicated primary analysis (Pike & Scott 1963) is paywalled and Scott's own 1990 'reanalysis' could not be obtained.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the scanned text we hold of Scott 1978 at pp.19-23 (2.31-2.32), and the record's paraphrase (lexical pitch accent; per-morpheme underlying accent incl. unaccented and post-accenting morphemes; surface restraints; no weight criterion; no contrastive intonation) matches the source. Scott 1978 is the standard and most recent reference grammar of Fore and the best available account of its prosody; the only fuller treatment (Pike & Scott 1963) is older, same analyst, and summarized in the grammar. sources.quote: 'Accent, marked by an acute over the vowel (or over the first vowel of a diphthong), is included throughout for purposes of reference, though left unwritten in local Fore publications. Fore phonology is presented in detail by Nicholson and Nicholson (1962), and again by Scott (1978). Analysis of accent is given by Pike and Scott (1963), concerning which Pilch (1970) has made some remarks.' Entries carry lexically placed accent marks (N/S dialect forms).
sources.note: Accent-marked lexicon by the same author; confirms accent is lexically specified per entry (downloaded now).

sources.citation: Pilch, Herbert. 1970. Pike-Scott's analysis of Fore suprasegmentals. Kivung 3(2): 133-142. (Paper read at the Third Annual Congress of the Linguistic Society of Papua New Guinea.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Secondary/theoretical, no new data: 'Fore words are characterized by different pitch patterns... There are minimal pairs which differ audibly by pitch only. Pike and Scott hesitate whether to categorize these pitch patterns as tone or stress... What Pike-Scott call accent turns out to be stress manifested by phonetic parameters other than loudness' ... 'if we categorize the Fore accent as stress, then Fore is a language with distinctive word-stress'. Scott 1978 p.22 rebuts Pilch's 'exactly three pitch patterns' claim as misleading.
sources.locator: pp.133-135 (scanned text; PDF has no text layer)
sources.note: Theoretical reanalysis of the same facts as 'distinctive word-stress manifested by pitch'; relevant only to the tonal-vs-pitch accent-vs-stress label, already answered in Scott 1978 2.31.2 (downloaded now).
